Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Geometrically the derivative is the slope of the tangent, obtained as the limiting position of secants. The tangent is a first-order approximation, so it matches the curve to first order and may lie above or below it. A zero derivative gives a horizontal tangent, which is a candidate extremum but not a certainty, and the angle of inclination is $\tan^{-1}$ of the slope rather than the slope itself.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Tangent at $a$: $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x-a)$
Angle of inclination: $\tan\theta = f'(a)$
Stationary point: $f'(a)=0$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Computing $f'(a)$ and reporting it as the angle of inclination, forgetting to apply $\theta=\tan^{-1}(f'(a))$.  ·  Saying a horizontal tangent guarantees a maximum; it marks a candidate only.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Where a formula is quoted it is valid only under the conditions stated; Computing $f'(a)$ and reporting it as the angle of inclination, forgetting to apply $\theta=\tan^{-1}(f'(a))$.  ·  Every result here follows from the definitions, so a first-principles derivation is always a valid fallback in the exam.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The derivative is the tangent slope, obtained as a limit of chord slopes.  ·  A horizontal tangent marks a candidate extremum, not a guaranteed one.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Computing the normal's slope as $-\frac1{f'(a)}$ when $f'(a)=0$, which is division by zero — the normal is vertical instead.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Work through the authored practice problems and re-derive each key formula from the definition.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: If the question says 'angle of inclination', finish with $\tan^{-1}$ — reporting the raw slope loses the mark.  ·  Sketch the curve and mark the tangent; a picture settles sign and quadrant questions faster than algebra.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Finding the equation of a tangent or normal at a point is a standard 3-mark question.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Topic anchor: Normal lines are perpendicular to the tangent, so their slope is $- frac1{f'(a)}$, undefined when $f'(a)=0$ — precisely the case that gives a horizontal tangent and hence a VERTICAL normal.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Report an ANGLE, not a slope, when the question asks for the angle of inclination.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The tangent to a curve is the local linear model: an error of order $h^2$ in $x$ gives an error of order $h^2$ in the approximation, which is why linearising motion equations is the first step of most numerical simulation.  ·  Refraction can be derived by demanding the path length be stationary, which is Fermat's condition and a direct application of the horizontal-tangent principle.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **The derivative is the tangent slope.** $f'(a)$ is the slope of the tangent to $y=f(x)$ at $x=a$, obtained as the limit of chord slopes, so the tangent is the limiting position of secants as the second point approaches $a$.  ·  **The tangent touches but does not cross.** Since $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(h)$, the curve and its tangent agree to first order and differ only at second order. This is why the tangent line is a first-order approximation and why it may lie above or below the curve.  ·  **A horizontal tangent means a stationary point,** $f'(a)=0$, where the graph neither rises nor falls. This is the condition for a maximum or a minimum, but not a guarantee of one — $y=x^3$ has a horizontal tangent at the origin with no extremum.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Normal slope: $-\frac{1}{f'(a)}$ for $f'(a)\ne0$  ·  Expansion: $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(h)$  ·  Statement 1: $f'(a)$ is the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=a$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 2: $f'(a)=0$ indicates a horizontal tangent.  ·  Statement 3: The angle of inclination satisfies $\tan\theta=f'(a)$.  ·  Statement 4: A horizontal tangent makes the normal vertical, so the normal has no finite slope.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 5: The tangent line agrees with the curve to first order near the point of contact.  ·  **The angle of inclination satisfies $\tan\theta = f'(a)$**, so a negative derivative corresponds to an obtuse angle when measured counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Questions often ask for the angle, requiring this extra step.  ·  **Parallel curves have equal derivatives at equal $x$:** if $f'(a)=g'(a)$ the tangents are parallel, and the vertical gap between the curves is stationary there. This is used to compare solutions of competing processes.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Normal lines are perpendicular to the tangent,** so their slope is $-\frac1{f'(a)}$, undefined when $f'(a)=0$ — precisely the case that gives a horizontal tangent and hence a VERTICAL normal.
